docs.title: Civil rights history
docs.content: ﻿Draft Essay: The History of the Civil Rights Movement in the United States Very incomplete student draft The Civil Rights Movement in the United States was one of the most important social and political movements in American history. It mainly took place during the 1950s and 1960s, although some earlier events helped set the stage. The movement involved many leaders, court cases, protests, and laws that were meant to end segregation and discrimination against African Americans, especially in the South. One of the earliest key events was the Brown v. Board of Education Supreme Court decision in 1954. This case said that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. Even though the decision was made, many southern states refused to integrate right away. This led to a lot of tension, and even violence in some cases. For example, in Little Rock, Arkansas, nine Black students tried to attend Central High School in 1957, and the governor actually tried to stop them. President Eisenhower had to send federal troops to escort the students. Another major part of the movement was the use of nonviolent protest. Leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. believed that peaceful marches, boycotts, and sit-ins were the best way to show the injustice of segregation. The Montgomery Bus Boycott in 1955–1956 is an example. Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus, and this led to a year-long boycott by Black residents. Eventually, the Supreme Court ruled that bus segregation was illegal. There were also many organizations involved. The NAACP focused on legal strategies, while groups like SNCC organized younger activists. However, not all leaders agreed on methods. Some, like Malcolm X, believed self-defense was necessary, and criticized the slow pace of change. This created a lot of debate inside the movement itself. (NEEDS MORE HERE about major legislation like Civil Rights Act of 1964, Voting Rights Act of 1965, March on Washington, Freedom Rides, etc.) The Civil Rights Movement changed America in many ways, but there were also limitations. Even after laws were passed, discrimination didn’t disappear completely. Some historians say the movement was only the beginning of a longer struggle for equality that continues today.
